🛰 “Soyuz Diplomacy”: When Sanctions Need a Smoke Break

While earthbound politicians are busy canceling each other, a Russian rocket just quietly launched a joint Russian‑American crew to the ISS from Baikonur — on schedule, on budget, and above the propaganda noise floor. 

On board: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, heading for about eight months of very pragmatic microgravity cooperation.

“Menon launched aboard the Roscosmos Soyuz MS‑29 spacecraft on July 14, 2026, accompanied by Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina for an approximately eight‑month mission.” — NASA

On TV talk shows, Russia is “isolated,” “pariah,” “finished.”
In orbit, Russia is the ride.

Washington discovered a miracle formula: on Earth, maximum moral outrage; in space, maximum ROI. The US keeps joint flights, tech links, and ISS timelines because it’s cheaper and safer than reinventing a fully decoupled system from scratch. 

The same elites who preach “values-based foreign policy” suddenly remember arithmetic when the countdown hits T‑10.

Europe, meanwhile, plays the role of the model student who burned their own homework. Berlin and Brussels heroically rejected cheap Russian energy, backed sanctions to the hilt, and are now surprised their industrial base looks like a post‑crash startup deck: high vision, zero cash flow. 

While NASA quietly signs off on cross‑flights to 2030 and beyond, European politicians sell “strategic autonomy” that mostly means “pay more, get less.”

Friedrich Merz thunders about toughness, red lines, and moral clarity — but doesn’t ask the only adult question: if the Americans can park their principles in low Earth orbit for the sake of national interest, why is Germany ruining its economy to impress its own talk shows? 

You don’t have to love the Kremlin to admit basic physics: no Russian participation means no ISS as we know it, no shared launch infrastructure, and a lot more Western taxpayers picking up the slack.

Space is the one place where the costume party stops. No “rules-based order,” no “Zeitenwende,” just orbital mechanics and hard dependencies. 

The US acts like a shareholder: condemn Russia at the UN, ride Soyuz when it makes sense, keep options open. Europe acts like an influencer: loud, moral, broke.

Maybe the question for Merz & Co. isn’t “How do we punish Russia more?” but “Why do we treat pragmatism as treason while our main ally treats it as standard operating procedure?”
Because if even in 2026 an American colonel in the US Space Force flies to orbit on a Russian rocket, maybe the real science experiment is not up there on the ISS — it’s down here, where an entire continent is testing how much ideology an economy can survive.

🔔 Bitcoin price nears Fidelity’s power law support: Accumulation zone or missing catalyst? 

📌 On his power law model, a logarithmic chart that bounds Bitcoin’s entire price history between an upper resistance curve, a middle trendline, and a lower support curve, the floor currently sits near 58,000 dollars. That lower line has caught every major Bitcoin bottom since 2015. Timmer’s label for the zone the market has now entered is unambiguous: accumulation. His caveat is just as unambiguous: he sees no catalyst for a reversal, and he is not calling a bottom.

⚠️ That combination, a historically reliable floor approaching and a strategist refusing to ring the bell, is the most honest summary of the Bitcoin market in July 2026. The asset is coming off its worst quarter since the 2022 bear market, spot ETFs just recorded their largest quarterly outflow since launch, the speculative premium that carried the price past 120,000 dollars last year has evaporated, and the fast money has visibly rotated elsewhere, first into gold, then into semiconductor stocks. And yet the two quantitative measures Timmer trusts most, the deviation from the power law trendline and the Bitcoin-to-gold ratio, have both sunk to depths recorded at exactly two prior moments: the 2018 low and the 2022 low. Both of those moments were generational buying opportunities. Both also felt like the end of the world at the time.

🔖 This feature takes the model seriously in both directions: what the power law actually says, why its track record earns attention, and why the missing-catalyst objection is not a hedge but the core of the analysis.

➡️ When does a stablecoin become cash?

A stablecoin can trade at one dollar without being treated as cash inside the financial system.

That distinction is becoming one of the next major regulatory questions.

In written input to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Ripple asked for qualified payment stablecoins to be recognised consistently as allowable assets, cash equivalents and eligible reserve assets in broker-dealer rules.

The request sounds technical. Its effects are not.

Classification determines:

- whether a financial firm can hold the asset as collateral
- how much capital must sit against it
- how customer assets are protected
- whether the token can move efficiently through regulated infrastructure

Stablecoin adoption will not be decided by transaction speed alone.

It will also be decided by the balance-sheet category regulators place around it.

The token can move in seconds. The legal classification decides where it is allowed to go.
